fetched_contents.text: Corrosion Resistance of Basalt Fiber Reinforced Composites for Marine Applications: Investigation of Mechanical Properties in Acidic, Alkaline, and Seawater Environments This review summarizes current research examining the corrosion resistance, aging behavior, and mechanical properties of basalt fiber-reinforced polymer (BFTP) composites in marine applications. Naturally derived basalt fiber offers a strong alternative to glass and carbon fibers thanks to its high strength, thermal/chemical stability, low cost, and environmentally friendly structure. Findings indicate that BFTP composites exhibit high corrosion resistance, particularly in challenging environments such as acidic and seawater, and offer superior performance to vinylester resin systems. Surface treatments with silane, zircon, nanotubes, and metal additives also significantly enhance mechanical and corrosion resistance. BFTP composites, which have proven successful in marine hulls, propellers, and structural components, stand out for their low water absorption, high tensile/flexural strength, good fatigue resistance, and high-temperature resistance. Life cycle analyses indicate that they offer a lower carbon footprint compared to glass fiber composites. These properties make BFTP composites a sustainable and cost-effective alternative material for the maritime industry. Danilo D'Andrea Fabio Salmeri Giacomo Risitano Guido Di Bella The increasing demand for environmentally friendly materials has driven researchers and industries to explore alternatives that combine performance with reduced environmental impact. In this framework, the possibility of replacing glass-fibre-reinforced composites (GFRCs) with basalt-fibre-reinforced composites (BFRCs) is attracting increasing attention. In this study, basalt–vinyl ester specimens and glass–vinyl ester specimens were mechanically characterized using both the Risitano Thermographic and Static Thermographic Methods. The results indicate that energy methods are effective for the mechanical characterization of complex materials like basalt and glass fibre composites. The average ultimate tensile strength was 374 ± 20.2 MPa for BFRCs and 295 ± 4.7 MPa for GFRCs, showing a 26.7% improvement with basalt. The fatigue limit was 96.5 ± 0.2 MPa for BFRCs and 104.8 ± 0.8 MPa for GFRCs, while the static stress limit estimated via thermography was 99.9 ± 6.45 MPa and 101.7 ± 5.24 MPa, respectively. Furthermore, the failure mechanisms of both BFRC and GFRC specimens were investigated. Additionally, a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) was performed to evaluate the environmental impact of basalt and glass fibre composites. The results showed that BFRCs have lower environmental impacts, including 0.67 kg CO2-eq with respect to climate change versus 0.81 kg CO2-eq for GFRCs. This work highlights how the two materials are comparable in terms of their mechanical performance but different in terms of their sustainability and environmental impact. Three-point flexural tests with different spans were conducted to evaluate the flexural behavior and fracture mechanisms. The best-performing configuration, based on glass fibers and vacuum infusion, achieved a maximum flexural strength of about 500 MPa, while basalt-based laminates reached values of up to 400 MPa. Basalt laminates exhibited the highest flexural modulus, with values exceeding 24 GPa. An increase in span length from 120 mm to 220 mm resulted in a reduction in flexural strength of approximately 6–18% depending on the laminate configuration, highlighting the influence of loading conditions on mechanical behavior. PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC7664919 PMID: 33182273 Abstract Basalt fibers have been adopted as reinforcements to improve mechanical performance of concrete materials and structures due to their excellent corrosion resistance, affordable cost, and environmental-friendly nature. While the reinforcing efficiency is significantly dependent on fiber–matrix interfacial properties, there is a lack of studies focusing on the bonding behavior of basalt fibers in the mortar matrix. In this paper, a series of experiments were carried out to investigate the characteristics of single basalt fiber pulled out from the mortar matrix. Three embedment lengths and three types of mortar strength were considered. As references, the pull-out behavior of single polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) fiber and glass fiber in mortar matrix were also tested for comparison. Results from the pull-out test revealed that the average bonding strength is more effective than the equivalent shear bonding strength to illustrate the interfacial bond behavior of single basalt fiber in mortar matrix, which can be improved by either longer embedment length or the stronger mortar matrix. Finally, the tensile and compressive strengths of basalt/PVA/glass fiber-reinforced concrete (FRC) were measured to investigate the influence of interfacial shear bonding strengths. It was shown that, while PVA fiber developed the highest shear bonding strength with mortar, the basalt fiber exhibited the best reinforcing efficiency of FRC. Introduction Basalt fiber, as a natural material on earth, has recently received increasing attention for reinforcement in composites used in civil, aerospace, and electronic engineering. Basalt fiber is derived from volcanic rocks with a melting temperature between 1500 and 1700 °C [1,2]. In comparison to carbon and glass fibers, production of basalt fiber requires less energy without gas emission, reducing its environmental impact and cost significantly [3,4]. Moreover, when compared with the traditional fibers (e.g., steel, glass and carbon fibers), basalt fiber not only has an environmental-friendly manufacturing process [5], but also exhibits attractive properties, such as high tensile strength and elastic modulus [1], satisfactory adhesion strength [6], excellent acid and alkaline resistance [7], high thermal stability [2], and renewability [8]. In recent years, applications of basalt fiber in civil engineering have gained increasing interest, such as basalt fiber-reinforced polymer bars to substitute steel bars in reinforced concrete [9,10] and chopped fiber-filled cementitious materials [11,12]. Introduction Concrete is a composite material with high compressive strength but relatively low tensile strength and a low energy absorption capacity. Improving the properties of concrete has become one of the most important challenges over the last decades. Implementing fibers into a concrete mixture, in general, improves mechanical properties such as tensile, flexural, and improved toughness strength as well as reducing the brittleness of the concrete. There are various commercially available fibers for use, such as steel, glass, synthetic and natural materials. Steel fibers are the most common type of fibers being utilized (50% of the total used fibers), followed by polypropylene (PP) fibers (20% of total used fibers), glass fibers (5% of total used fibers) and lastly other types of fibers (25% of total used fibers) [1]. Many research works [2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9] have been carried out to investigate the effect of using fibers on the behavior of reinforced concrete. These studies brought awareness of the improvement in mechanical properties, durability, and fracture resistance of the concrete composite from the addition of fibers. Studies have shown that Fiber-Reinforced Concrete (FRC) is primarily dependent on the properties and dispersion of the fibers in the concrete matrix [10,11,12,13]. The main characteristics to be considered are: the fiber material properties, fiber geometry, fiber distribution/orientation and fiber concentration [14,15,16]. The properties of the fiber material being used, such as: modulus of elasticity, tensile strength, and strain at failure, are crucial when developing an FRC mix. Fibers with high modulus, such as steel fibers, have been shown to simultaneously improve both flexural and impact resistance. On the other hand, fibers with low modulus, such as polypropylene, have been shown to improve toughness and early age cracking, but do not contribute much to concrete flexural strength. Fiber geometry is another important fiber characteristic to take into account. This includes properties such as: fiber length, diameter, aspect ratio (L/D), cross section shape and presence or absence of hooks at the ends of the fibers [17,18,19]. Fiber lengths may range from 6 mm to 150 mm (0.25 inch. to 6 inch.) and thicknesses ranging from 0.005 mm to 0.75 mm. (0.0002 inch. to 0.03 inch.). The literature has shown that longer fibers tends to bridge cracks better and improved flexural strength can be obtained by increasing the aspect ratio [20]. However, utilizing a high aspect ratio fiber increases the potential for balling of the fibers creating further workability problems within the mix. Microfibers, on the other hand, have been shown to be most effective at increasing performance parameters, such as plastic shrinkage, during early stages of crack formation [21,22]. Fiber concentration is another fiber characteristic that affects the effectiveness of the fibers in the cement matrix, and it is measured as a percentage of the total volume of the composite (concrete and fibers). Low fiber volumes (<1%) are typically used to control plastic shrinkage, crack propagation control and crack width reduction but displays no significant improvement in strength [23,24]. Medium fiber volumes (1–2%) have been shown to be applicable to supplement the main reinforcement in the member in order to provide improved mechanical properties such as toughness and crack control, and they are typically used in cast-in-place or precast FRC members [25,26,27,28]. High fiber volumes (>2%) are mainly used for structures that require improved toughness, enhanced ductility, and improved fracture energy [29,30]. Although the fiber volume changes with the type of application, the main use of fibers is to improve the brittleness of the concrete, toughness, crack propagation and reduction in crack width. However, the use of fibers is not to replace the main reinforcement in the members, but rather enhance certain mechanical characteristics within the member utilizing the fibers as a bridging mechanism. Iyer et al. [11] investigated the effect of using basalt fibers with volume fractions between 0.1 and 0.5%. The results showed that, increasing fiber content significantly decreases the workability. Therefore, it is recommended that the fiber content remains below 0.5%. Similarly, the mechanical properties of basalt fibers concrete BFC, with fiber content between 0.25% and 0.75%, have been investigated by Yang et al. [12]. The results showed that the optimum strength is produced by fiber volumes between 0.3% and 0.5%. In return, in this study, basalt fibers have been used with volume fractions between 0.15% and 0.5%. In the literature, it has been reported that steel fibers are the most common type of fibers used due to its high modulus of elasticity; in addition, it improves the different mechanical properties of concrete mixtures [4,9]. Moreover, Eisa et al. [9] found that, including steel fibers, with a 1% volume fraction, into conventional concrete improved the modulus of elasticity by 30%, the modulus of rupture by 26%, and the splitting tensile strength by 96%. In addition, using steel fibers did not show a considerable improvement on the compressive strength of the concrete. Studies [31,32] have shown that the optimum steel fiber content, to improve the mechanical properties of concrete, is between 0.25% and 1.00%. In return, in this study, steel fiber was incorporated into BFC with volume fractions of 0.3% and 0.5% to maintain the total volume of fibers at less than 1%. Fibers made from steel, polypropylene and glass are currently the most common fiber types used to produce fiber-reinforced concrete and they have been investigated and used for decades. How bonding strength affects basalt fiber design

Interfacial bonding is central to how basalt fibers transfer load to the matrix in composite structures. The evidence shows that the interphase region between inclusions and a polymer matrix plays an important role in determining interfacial bonding strength in polymer composites [N2-R1]. In basalt fiber composites, the interface interaction between the fiber and the matrix directly affects the mechanical properties of the composite material [N2-R2]. This means that stronger interfacial bonding improves load transfer from the fiber to the matrix, which is essential for maintaining mechanical performance under stress [N2-R2].

Coating properties that maximize bonding strength are shaped by both fiber-matrix chemistry and surface treatment. Surface activation and characterization of basalt fiber by plasma modification aimed to investigate the effects of low-pressure plasma modification on the interfacial adhesion property between basalt fiber and the matrix [N2-R4]. Similarly, inorganic silicon dioxide nanoparticles were deposited on continuous basalt fibers to enhance interfacial adhesion [N2-R5]. These findings suggest that surface treatments and functional coatings can improve bonding strength by altering the fiber surface to promote better adhesion with the matrix [N2-R4][N2-R5]. The evidence also indicates that interfacial bonding strength is more effectively described by average bonding strength than by equivalent shear bonding strength in pull-out tests, implying that bonding strength is a key indicator of load-transfer behavior rather than just shear resistance alone [N2-F2].

Bonding strength directly influences failure modes and service life. The evidence on failure mechanisms of plain glass and basalt fiber-reinforced composites shows that composites can fail due to matrix cracking, delamination, fiber breakage, and debonding from mechanical forces [N7-R3]. In addition, hygrothermal ageing effects on flexural, interlaminar shear, and in-plane shear properties and associated failure modes were analyzed in a study, showing that failure modes are strongly dependent on environmental exposure and aging [N7-R4]. For basalt fiber-reinforced composites, the literature also suggests that mechanical performance depends on fiber-matrix interfacial properties [N2-R2]. Therefore, weaker bonding strength increases the likelihood of debonding, delamination, or matrix cracking during service, which shortens service life [N7-R3].

Overall, bonding strength is not just a mechanical property but a design constraint: it determines how well the fiber can carry load, which coating treatments can optimize, and which failure modes are most likely under service conditions. The evidence supports the conclusion that better bonding strength improves load transfer, enhances mechanical performance, and delays failure, while poor bonding can compromise both service life and structural reliability [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N7-R3].
node_outputs.N8:
How chemical corrosion resistance affects basalt fiber design

Basalt fiber coatings are intended to resist corrosive environments that would otherwise degrade the fiber or matrix. The evidence indicates that basalt fibers show superior resistance to corrosion and chemical attack compared to glass and carbon fibers, and they withstand alkalis, acids, and other aggressive environments [N1-R5]. Marine and seawater environments are especially relevant: findings indicate that basalt fiber-reinforced polymer (BFTP) composites exhibit high corrosion resistance, particularly in acidic and seawater environments, and offer superior performance to vinylester resin systems [N1-F1]. This suggests that coating design is often targeted at marine, coastal, or chemically aggressive environments where unprotected basalt fibers would degrade [N1-F1][N1-R5].

Coating composition and thickness influence corrosion resistance through material selection and barrier function. Surface treatments with silane, zircon, nanotubes, and metal additives significantly enhance mechanical and corrosion resistance [N1-F1]. Silane coupling agents are explicitly described as acting like a bridge between basalt fillers and organic resins to enhance mechanical properties and chemical durability [N1-R1]. The evidence also notes that corrosion resistance can vary by basalt type: calc-alkaline basalt fiber shows better corrosion resistance than alkali basalt fiber [N1-R2]. This implies that coating composition is not just a passive layer but can be tailored with functional additives or surface treatments to improve resistance to specific corrosive species [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R2].

Tradeoffs between coating durability and other design factors are evident in the evidence. Basalt fibers are naturally corrosion-resistant, but in practical applications, coatings are added to enhance this resistance further [N1-F1]. At the same time, the evidence indicates that basalt fiber production is more cost-effective than glass fiber production because it requires no chemical additives and uses much less energy [N6-R4]. This suggests that coating durability must be balanced against cost, manufacturability, and environmental impact [N6-R4]. In marine applications, BFTP composites stand out for low water absorption, high tensile/flexural strength, good fatigue resistance, and high-temperature resistance, but they also require lifecycle assessment to evaluate environmental impact [N1-F1]. So, while better corrosion resistance improves service life and performance, it may require more complex coatings, higher material costs, or additional processing steps [N1-F1][N6-R4].

In summary, chemical corrosion resistance affects basalt fiber design by dictating the corrosive environments the coating must protect against, by determining which coating materials and treatments can enhance durability, and by requiring tradeoffs with cost, manufacturability, and environmental impact [N1-R5][N1-F1][N1-R1][N6-R4].
node_outputs.N12:
Application-specific design choices shaped by coating properties

Applications prioritize corrosion resistance versus bonding strength depending on the service environment and structural demands. For marine and corrosive environments, the evidence strongly supports prioritizing corrosion resistance because basalt fiber-reinforced polymer (BFTP) composites exhibit high corrosion resistance, particularly in acidic and seawater environments [N1-F1]. In contrast, applications where load transfer and mechanical performance are critical may prioritize bonding strength. The evidence shows that the interface interaction between basalt fiber and matrix directly affects mechanical properties [N2-R2], and that interfacial bonding strength determines load transfer from fiber to matrix [N2-R1]. Therefore, in high-load or high-stress applications, bonding strength is more important than corrosion resistance alone [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Environmental exposure dictates coating selection by defining the corrosive or aggressive conditions the coating must resist. The evidence indicates that corrosion resistance is especially important in marine, acidic, and seawater environments [N1-F1], while also noting that calc-alkaline basalt fiber shows better corrosion resistance than alkali basalt fiber [N1-R2]. Surface treatments such as silane, zircon, nanotubes, and metal additives are specifically used to enhance mechanical and corrosion resistance [N1-F1]. This means that coatings are selected not just by general durability but by the specific environmental threats present in the application [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Manufacturing and cost constraints shape coating design because basalt fibers are already attractive for low cost and low energy production [N6-R4]. The evidence also states that basalt fiber production is more cost-effective than glass fiber production because it requires no chemical additives and uses much less energy [N6-R4]. At the same time, the evidence shows that coating composition and thickness can be optimized to enhance performance [N1-F1][N1-R1]. Therefore, design choices are constrained by the need to balance coating performance with manufacturability, scalability, and cost [N6-R4][N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means that applications with tight cost limits may favor simpler or cheaper coatings, while applications requiring long-term durability may justify more expensive or complex treatments [N6-R4][N1-F1].

Overall, coating properties determine whether a design emphasizes corrosion resistance, bonding strength, or a combination of both. The evidence supports the conclusion that environmental exposure defines the coating’s protective function, while manufacturing and cost constraints shape how that protection is implemented [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R4].
node_outputs.N10:
Coating-material tradeoffs and practical design constraints

The most commonly used coating materials for basalt fiber appear to be those that combine chemical durability, mechanical compatibility, and functional surface treatment. The evidence highlights silane coupling agents as a common choice because they act as a bridge between basalt fillers and organic resins, enhancing mechanical properties and chemical durability [N1-R1]. Silane is also mentioned explicitly in the marine corrosion study as a surface treatment that significantly enhances mechanical and corrosion resistance [N1-F1]. Epoxy and polyurethane are also relevant in the context of fiber-matrix composites, with epoxy composites being discussed in relation to interfacial adhesion and mechanical properties [N3-R3]. Polyurethane is also referenced in a study that used basalt microfibers and polyurethane elastomer as matrix materials [N3-R2]. These materials are common because they provide good compatibility with fibers and can be modified to improve adhesion and durability [N3-R2][N3-R3][N1-R1].

Cost, scalability, and manufacturability constrain coating choice because basalt fiber production itself is described as more cost-effective than glass fiber production, using less energy and requiring no chemical additives [N6-R4]. The same source also notes that the price of basalt fiber varies significantly depending on its form, manufacturing complexity, and technical specifications [N6-R1]. This implies that coating materials must be chosen in a way that aligns with production economics and industrial scalability. For example, simpler coatings may be favored when cost and manufacturability are tighter constraints, while more complex surface treatments may be justified in applications where performance gains are substantial [N6-R1][N6-R4].

Coating thickness and application method affect performance because the evidence shows that interfacial bonding strength can be improved by longer embedment length or stronger mortar matrix in pull-out tests [N2-F2]. Although this is not directly about coating thickness, it reflects a broader principle: the thickness and application method of a coating can influence load transfer and interfacial behavior. The evidence also notes that surface treatments with silane, zircon, nanotubes, and metal additives significantly enhance mechanical and corrosion resistance [N1-F1], suggesting that even small changes in coating composition or thickness can have large performance effects [N1-F1]. Therefore, practical design must balance coating thickness and application method with the desired level of durability, bonding strength, and cost [N2-F2][N1-F1][N6-R1].

In conclusion, the most common coating materials for basalt fiber are silane-based treatments, epoxy, and polyurethane, because they enhance mechanical and chemical durability while being compatible with fiber-matrix systems [N1-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. However, cost, scalability, and manufacturability constrain their selection, and coating thickness and application method must be optimized to achieve the desired performance without excessive complexity or cost [N6-R1][N6-R4][N2-F2].

Long-term behavior and service-life consequences of coated basalt fibers

Failure modes triggered by coating and fiber interaction include delamination, debonding, matrix cracking, and other interfacial failures. The evidence shows that composites can fail due to matrix cracking, delamination, fiber breakage, and debonding from mechanical forces [N7-R3]. It also notes that failure mechanisms of plain glass and basalt fiber-reinforced composites and a selected glass/basalt hybrid composite sequence were evaluated [N7-R5]. This indicates that long-term service behavior is governed not only by the fiber itself but also by how the coating or matrix interacts with the fiber over time [N7-R3][N7-R5].

Degradation over time can change both corrosion resistance and bonding strength. The evidence indicates that surface treatments with silane, zircon, nanotubes, and metal additives significantly enhance mechanical and corrosion resistance [N1-F1]. However, degradation can reduce these benefits if the coating or fiber-matrix interface is compromised. The marine study also reports that BFTP composites exhibit low water absorption, which helps maintain long-term durability, but it also notes that mechanical performance and environmental impact must be evaluated through lifecycle assessment [N1-F1]. This implies that initial corrosion resistance and bonding strength can degrade with aging, moisture, or chemical exposure, reducing service life [N1-F1][N7-R4]. Hygrothermal ageing effects were specifically analyzed for flexural, interlaminar shear, and in-plane shear properties and associated failure modes, showing that aging changes failure behavior [N7-R4].

Service life is predicted or assessed through mechanical testing, failure analysis, and lifecycle evaluation. The evidence includes studies that measured tensile and compressive strengths of basalt fiber-reinforced concrete to investigate the influence of interfacial shear bonding strengths [N2-F2]. It also reports that energy methods are effective for mechanical characterization of complex materials like basalt and glass fiber composites [N1-F1]. The lifecycle assessment in the marine study shows that BFRCs have lower environmental impacts than GFRCs, and that mechanical performance must be balanced against sustainability [N1-F1]. Thus, practical assessment of service life involves both direct mechanical performance testing and broader lifecycle evaluation to account for long-term durability and environmental consequences [N2-F2][N1-F1][N7-R4].

Overall, coated basalt fibers are subject to failure modes such as delamination, debonding, matrix cracking, and fiber breakage, and their long-term performance depends on how degradation affects corrosion resistance and bonding strength [N7-R3][N7-R5]. Service life is therefore predicted through mechanical testing, failure analysis, and lifecycle assessment, rather than being assumed to remain constant over time [N2-F2][N1-F1][N7-R4].

These properties are not independent. In practice, the coating must protect the fiber from aggressive environments while also enabling strong fiber-matrix interaction, because both durability and mechanical performance depend on them. The evidence from the branch reports supports a unified design logic: coatings are chosen to match the environmental exposure, optimize interfacial bonding, balance cost and manufacturability, and withstand long-term degradation without compromising service life [N1-R5][N2-R1][N2-R2][N6-R4].

In practical applications, the design of basalt fiber coatings is shaped by a single logic: **coatings must protect the fiber from corrosion while also enabling strong bonding to the matrix**.
